top_story: By 14 July, three consecutive nights of US strikes on Iran had merged with a declared effort to reimpose naval control over the Strait of Hormuz, shifting the crisis from reciprocal attacks into a contest over who can regulate the Gulf’s economic lifeline. Iran answered by widening the battlespace beyond the waterway, including a ballistic missile strike on a US air base in Jordan, raising immediate risks for neighboring states, shipping flows, and populations already exposed to disruption and price shock. The earlier exchange of attacks around Hormuz now looks less like a discrete flare-up than the opening phase of a broader coercive campaign in which Washington is using maritime pressure and Tehran is testing regional escalation. The clearest takeaway is that control of commerce and civilian vulnerability, not only battlefield signaling, has become the central lever of this confrontation.
